items.topic: Dysphagia — thickened liquids slow flow to reduce aspiration risk; follow SLP orders
items.stem: An older adult with dysphagia is ordered nectar-thick liquids after a swallow evaluation. Which teaching best explains the purpose of thickened liquids?

options.text: Thickened liquids move more slowly, which can improve swallowing control and help reduce aspiration risk as directed by the speech-language pathologist
Thickened liquids permanently cure stroke-related dysphagia within 24 hours
Thickened liquids replace the need for upright positioning during meals
Any thin liquid is safer than thickened liquid for clients who cough when drinking

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: thickening increases viscosity so liquids move more slowly and improve swallowing; nurses collaborate with speech pathologists. OpenStax Med-Surg: thickened liquids and texture modification are primary methods to prevent aspiration in at-risk older adults.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Thickened liquids are a compensatory strategy, not a cure for dysphagia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Upright positioning remains an important aspiration-prevention strategy alongside texture modification.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Thin liquids often increase aspiration risk when dysphagia is present; the ordered thickened consistency is safer when indicated.

items.topic: NGN matrix — dysphagia thickened-liquid and aspiration precautions indicated vs not
items.stem: For an older adult ordered nectar-thick liquids after a swallow evaluation for aspiration risk, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Provide liquids at the ordered thickened consistency (nectar-thick)
Keep the client upright (at least 30 degrees) during oral intake
Collaborate with speech-language pathology on safe swallowing strategies
Offer thin water between thickened sips because 'a little thin liquid is always fine'
Tell the client to lie flat immediately while drinking to 'protect the airway'

rationales.R1: Indicated. Follow the prescribed thickened consistency to slow liquid flow and support safer swallowing.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Upright positioning during intake decreases aspiration risk.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Nurses collaborate with SLP for dysphagia diets and swallowing strategies.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Adding unauthorized thin liquids undermines the dysphagia plan and can increase aspiration risk.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Lying flat while drinking increases aspiration risk; upright positioning is preferred.

items.topic: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — stop all heparin; start nonheparin anticoagulant
items.stem: On day 7 of unfractionated heparin, a client's platelets fall by more than 50% and a new lower-extremity clot is suspected. Which action is the priority pending HIT evaluation?

options.text: Stop all heparin products immediately and anticipate a nonheparin anticoagulant per protocol/orders
Switch only to low-molecular-weight heparin because HIT never cross-reacts with LMWH
Double the heparin infusion rate to overcome platelet clumping
Ignore the platelet drop because HIT causes bleeding, not thrombosis

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: stop heparin immediately and use a non-heparin anticoagulant. Merck: stop heparin if platelets drop >50% or new thrombosis occurs; substitute a nonheparin agent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck: most HIT antibodies cross-react with LMWH, so LMWH is not an acceptable substitute.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Continuing/increasing heparin worsens the immune process and thrombosis risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. HIT is typically a prothrombotic state; bleeding is uncommon.

items.topic: NGN matrix — suspected HIT actions indicated vs not
items.stem: For suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelet drop >50% with possible new thrombosis while on heparin), indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Stop unfractionated heparin immediately (including heparin flushes if ordered/protocol)
Anticipate a nonheparin anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban) per protocol/provider orders
Notify the provider/anticoagulation team and obtain ordered HIT laboratory evaluation
Switch the client to enoxaparin (LMWH) as the preferred HIT treatment
Increase the heparin infusion rate to 'overcome' thrombocytopenia

rationales.R1: Indicated. All heparin exposure should be stopped when HIT is suspected.
rationales.R2: Indicated. A nonheparin anticoagulant is substituted until platelets recover.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Evaluation and coordinated management are required.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. LMWH usually cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is not used to treat HIT.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Continuing/increasing heparin is harmful in HIT.

items.topic: Malignant hyperthermia — stop triggering anesthetics/succinylcholine and give IV dantrolene
items.stem: During general anesthesia with a volatile agent and succinylcholine, a client develops rising end-tidal CO₂, jaw rigidity, and tachycardia. Which intervention set is the priority for suspected malignant hyperthermia?

options.text: Stop triggering volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine and administer IV dantrolene with rapid cooling/support per protocol
Continue the volatile anesthetic and give only an antipyretic tablet
Give a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker as first-line therapy instead of dantrolene
Ignore rising ETCO₂ because malignant hyperthermia never occurs after the first anesthetic exposure

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: stop volatile agents, give dantrolene, and cool rapidly. GeneReviews: discontinue potent inhalation agents and succinylcholine and give IV dantrolene promptly.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Triggering agents must be stopped; antipyretics are not the treatment for MH.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Calcium-channel blockers are avoided with dantrolene (hyperkalemia risk); dantrolene is the specific therapy.
rationales.D: Incorrect. MH can occur after prior uneventful anesthetics; rising ETCO₂ with rigidity/tachycardia is a classic early pattern.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — malignant hyperthermia: stop triggers + dantrolene; monitor ETCO2/temp/rigidity
items.stem: A client under volatile anesthesia develops rising end-tidal CO₂, masseter rigidity, and tachycardia. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Malignant hyperthermia crisis related to triggering anesthetics
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis without anesthesia
Resolved ankle sprain in clinic without airway issues

actions.text: Stop volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine (triggering agents) per protocol
Administer IV dantrolene and initiate rapid cooling/supportive care
Increase the volatile anesthetic concentration to deepen anesthesia only
Give verapamil as the first-line antidote instead of dantrolene
Discharge home without monitoring because fever is expected after surgery

parameters.text: End-tidal CO₂ / ventilation response and core temperature
Muscle rigidity and signs of rhabdomyolysis (e.g., dark urine, rising CK per labs)

rationales.K1: Correct. Rising ETCO₂, rigidity, and tachycardia after triggering anesthetics indicate MH.
rationales.A2: Correct. IV dantrolene plus rapid cooling/support are priority treatments.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Calcium-channel blockers are avoided; dantrolene is the specific therapy.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. MH is a life-threatening emergency requiring intensive monitoring.
rationales.P1: Correct. ETCO₂ and temperature guide response to therapy.
rationales.P2: Correct. Rigidity and rhabdomyolysis markers are key MH complications to track.

sources.section: Treatment of Malignant Hyperthermia
sources.evidence: Stop volatile agents; dantrolene; rapid cooling; monitor for hyperthermia, rigidity, rising ETCO2, rhabdomyolysis.

items.topic: Alcohol use disorder — give IV thiamine before (or with) IV glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
items.stem: A client with heavy alcohol use arrives hypoglycemic and is about to receive IV dextrose. Which action best prevents precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.text: Administer IV thiamine before (or concurrently with) the IV glucose/dextrose as ordered/protocol
Withhold all thiamine because vitamins worsen hypoglycemia
Give a large oral carbohydrate meal instead of any parenteral vitamins
Start a monoamine oxidase inhibitor before the dextrose infusion

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: give IV thiamine before IV glucose in alcohol use disorder because glucose can worsen thiamine deficiency. OpenStax: IV thiamine with dextrose helps prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Thiamine is protective; withholding it increases Wernicke risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Carbohydrate loading without thiamine can worsen deficiency; parenteral thiamine is indicated in at-risk clients.
rationales.D: Incorrect. MAOIs are unrelated and unsafe here.

items.topic: TeamSTEPPS CUS — Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue to escalate a patient-safety concern
items.stem: A nurse believes a planned action is unsafe and prior statements were not heard. Using TeamSTEPPS CUS, which sequence best escalates the concern?

options.text: State 'I am Concerned,' then 'I am Uncomfortable,' then 'This is a Safety issue,' and notify a supervisor if the safety issue is not acknowledged
Say only 'whatever you think' and document nothing
Use CUS for routine interpersonal disagreements about lunch breaks
Start with insults about competence instead of stating a safety concern

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ/AHA TeamSTEPPS: CUS = Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue; escalate to a supervisor if unresolved.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Silence fails mutual support and advocacy responsibilities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CUS is for urgent safety concerns, not routine interpersonal issues.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CUS uses structured assertive language focused on the safety issue, not personal attacks.

items.topic: Medication safety — verify identity with two identifiers; room number is not valid
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Before administering a scheduled oral medication, which identification method is correct?

options.text: Ask the client to state full name and date of birth, then compare with the armband and MAR (at least two identifiers)
Use room number alone because it uniquely identifies every client
Skip identification if the nurse recognizes the client's face from yesterday
Ask only for the client's favourite colour as the sole identifier

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax CNS/Fundamentals: use at least two identifiers such as name and DOB and compare to armband/MAR.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Room number is not a unique identifier and must not be used to confirm identity.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Identity must be confirmed every time medications are administered.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Favourite colour is not an approved patient identifier.

items.topic: Adult high-quality CPR — chest compression rate 100 to 120/min
items.stem: During adult CPR for pulseless cardiac arrest, which chest compression rate is recommended for high-quality CPR?

options.text: 100 to 120 compressions per minute
40 to 50 compressions per minute
20 compressions per minute with long pauses after every compression
200 to 240 compressions per minute without allowing chest recoil

rationales.A: Correct. AHA adult BLS: reasonable to perform compressions at 100 to 120/min. OpenStax: high-quality CPR uses 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Far too slow; minimize interruptions.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Excessively fast and without recoil is not high-quality CPR.
